Chapter 4: Choosing What Matters and Saying No
When you really consider how short life is, figuring out where to spend your time suddenly feels a lot more urgent, doesn’t it?
You just can’t keep telling yourself you’ll get to everything someday. Every choice you make—every “yes”—means saying “no” to something else, even if you don’t realize it right away.
Now, I know this isn’t the most comfortable truth. Most of us grow up thinking that saying yes is always the right thing to do. We’re taught to grab every opportunity, say yes to every request, and believe we can be everything to everyone. But here’s the catch: that way of living? It just leaves us overcommitted, exhausted, and stretched way too thin.
Maybe you’ve seen this play out yourself—or maybe you’re living it right now. You want to be helpful, so you agree to every project, every favor, every invitation. At first, it feels good. You feel needed, involved, and dependable. But after a while, the cost starts to show.
Suddenly, there’s barely any time to rest. Relationships slip down the priority list. The things that used to bring you joy get squeezed out by obligations. Days start to blur together, and you realize you’re running on empty—with no space left for yourself.
Learning to say no? That’s a skill, and honestly, it’s one most people find pretty tough at first. It means risking people’s disappointment. It means setting boundaries, even when it feels awkward. But here’s something important: saying no isn’t selfish. In fact, it’s actually a sign that you respect yourself enough to protect your time.
If the idea of saying no feels intimidating, try starting small. Maybe you skip a meeting that isn’t truly necessary. Maybe you turn down a favor that doesn’t really fit with what matters to you. And you know what? The world keeps turning. Each time you say no, it gets a little easier to see what’s really important.
Prioritizing isn’t just about cutting stuff out of your life. It’s about making room for what actually matters to you. That could be more time with family, working on something creative, or just giving yourself permission to rest. What’s meaningful is different for everyone, but the bottom line stays the same: you only get so much time, and you get to choose how to use it.
This way of living takes honesty—with yourself and with others. It means admitting that you can’t do it all, and that’s perfectly okay. Sure, people might be disappointed sometimes, but the alternative—trying to please everyone—only leads to burnout and regret.
Over time, saying no stops feeling like you’re missing out. Instead, it becomes an act of self-care. It’s how you honor your limits and make the most of the life you’ve got. Depth ends up meaning a whole lot more than breadth. And at the end of the day, the best lives are the ones shaped by intention—by choosing what truly matters, and letting the rest fall away.
